site.title: CS2 Movement Guide
site.tagline: Learn standard CS2 movement, one technique at a time, from first strafe to map routes.
site.description: A CS2 movement guide covering ground movement, air control, jumps, ladders, surfs, advanced tricks, map routes and KZ.

body.text: Most clips in this guide were recorded in [[movement-hub|Movement Hub]], a free Steam Workshop map that lets you practise on the real competitive maps. Download it before you start.

In CS2, go to Play, then Workshop Maps, then pick Movement Hub.
Choose a map and use Free Roam to practise at your own pace, or Time Trial to race a route.

sections.title: Bind the scroll wheel to jump
sections.summary: Scroll wheel jump binds make bunny hops and tight jumps easier.

body.text: Everyone should jump with the scroll wheel. A wheel click can repeat faster than a key press, which matters for [[bhop|bunny hops]] and tight jumps. Open the [[console|console]] (turn it on in Settings, Game, Enable Developer Console) and paste:
`bind mwheeldown +jump`
`bind mwheelup +jump`
You can set several binds at once. This line keeps space and both wheel directions on jump, which helps if your wheel is worn:
`bind space +jump; bind mwheeldown +jump; bind mwheelup +jump`
Binds reset when you restart the game unless you put them in an [[autoexec|autoexec]]. See the Autoexec section below.

categories.title: Movement fundamentals
categories.intro: What speed, ticks and surfaces mean before you try anything.

sections.title: Velocity and momentum
sections.summary: The speed and direction you carry from one movement phase into the next.

body.text: Velocity is a vector. It has a magnitude (speed) and a direction. Horizontal velocity describes travel across the map; vertical velocity describes rising or falling. A speed number alone cannot tell you which way you are travelling. Two attempts can show the same speed while following different paths.

Read the HUD at four points: before takeoff, at the first air strafe, at the fastest point and after landing. `cl_showpos 1` can expose position, velocity and view information in a local practice session. Compare the velocity components when available, not just the rounded speed display.

When you lose distance, find the first phase that differs from a successful attempt. A poor approach changes takeoff speed; a bad first strafe changes the flight path; a late crouch can catch the target edge; a hard landing can apply a speed penalty. The final miss is often only the last symptom.

items: Separate horizontal speed from vertical velocity and facing direction.
Record pre-speed, peak speed, takeoff angle, landing position and post-landing speed.
Keep the map, server mode, start marker and input sequence fixed between trials.
Do not call a camera turn an acceleration event unless the velocity readout changes.

media.caption: Velocity and momentum

sections.title: Reading your speed
sections.summary: Use a velocity display instead of guessing by feel.

body.text: The developer console command `cl_showpos 1` displays position and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] information in the game. The exact on-screen layout can change, but the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] readout is useful for comparing attempts made under the same conditions.

For a fair comparison, use the same weapon, map, server, starting position and route. Note horizontal speed separately from vertical motion where the display provides both. A single peak number does not tell you whether you can control the landing or repeat the result.

If your practice map provides a movement HUD, use it to compare takeoff speed, maximum speed and the speed you carry into the landing. Treat plugin labels as that server’s measurement system, not as Valve’s official terminology.

items: Compare two attempts with the same starting conditions.
Watch whether speed changes during the ground run, in the air and at landing.
Record repeatable results rather than one lucky peak.

sections.title: Ground acceleration and friction
sections.summary: Why running builds or preserves speed, and why ground contact can remove it.

body.text: Ground movement changes speed through acceleration while an input is held and friction when the player is on the ground. Friction acts during contact, so a landing can remove speed even when your camera and keys appear to remain unchanged.

The useful run-up is the one that produces the required takeoff [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and angle. A straight run is easiest to measure. A diagonal or curved approach can create a better line for a particular jump, but it can also leave you with less speed in the direction of the target.

items: Use a fixed start and measure speed at the same takeoff mark.
Compare straight and diagonal run-ups separately.
Avoid unnecessary key overlaps when changing direction.

sections.title: Ticks, inputs and subtick
sections.summary: How CS2 records input timing and why old tick-perfect advice can be misleading.

body.text: CS2 accepts movement input with subtick timing. A button press or release can be represented at a point within a simulation tick, which matters for landings, crouch transitions and other frame-sensitive movement.

A subtick input system does not mean that every mechanical outcome is perfectly continuous or independent of client frame rate. The exact order in which input changes are processed can matter. Community reverse-engineering of CS2 bhopping shows that an extra input close to landing can split a movement step and change whether a hop is treated as perfect or restored.

Valve documented several relevant changes: in September 2025 it improved timestep-independence for subtick movement acceleration; in January 2026 it changed landing-time calculations and the [[bhop|bhop]] acceptance window. Those are reasons to prefer current CS2 demonstrations over copied CS:GO tick counts.

items: Record the game build and server mode.
Keep frame rate stable during A/B tests.
Change one input timing at a time.

sections.title: Surfaces and collision
sections.summary: The shape of the world matters as much as your inputs.

body.text: Player movement is resolved against map collision geometry. Floors, ramps, walls, ledges and corners can change whether you are grounded, sliding, blocked or airborne. A tiny difference in contact position can produce a different result in a precision movement attempt.

Valve has issued movement-related fixes involving surfing, excessive speed near walls and air-strafe [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. Those patch notes are a reminder that collision and movement edge cases can change between builds.

sections.title: Common mistakes, small corrections and practice habits
sections.summary: A checklist for making movement attempts repeatable and diagnosing avoidable errors.

body.text: A movement attempt contains several linked phases: line-up, approach, takeoff, air control, contact and recovery. A mistake early in the sequence can look like a problem with the final jump. Review the earliest point where your successful and failed attempts begin to differ.

When practising air strafes, avoid adding extra keys out of habit. Learn the movement sequence for the specific drill first, then add forward, backward or crouch inputs only when the route calls for them. See [[air-strafing|air strafing]], [[backwards-air|backward air control]] and [[crouch-jump|jump-crouch timing]].

items: Use the same start marker, map, server and movement mode for comparisons.
Change only one thing at a time: run-up, takeoff point, mouse arc, crouch or jump timing.
Record a full attempt, including the setup and landing.
Do not compare attempts made with different movement rules or server settings.
Check patch dates when an old route behaves differently.
Use a current clip with a visible keyboard overlay before copying a precise route.

categories.intro: Moving, stopping and taking off on the ground.

sections.title: Basic directional movement
sections.summary: W, A, S and D create a desired movement direction relative to your view.

body.text: W moves toward the direction you face, S moves away, and A/D move sideways relative to your view. Combining keys creates diagonal movement. The direction you look and the direction you travel are related, but they are not the same thing once you have [[velocity-momentum|momentum]].
Use simple routes first. Make one controlled turn, watch how your path changes, then add a second turn. Avoid holding every direction key while trying to understand a single mechanic.

items: Run forward, turn your view, and notice that your movement path does not instantly follow the crosshair.
Test diagonal movement with W+A and W+D.
Use A/D for side movement relative to your current view, not relative to the map.

sections.title: Counter-strafing
sections.summary: Tap the opposite direction to stop before firing.

body.text: Counter-strafing means applying an opposite movement input to cancel existing ground [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. If you are moving right with D, a brief A input accelerates you back toward a stop. Reverse the inputs when moving left.
The goal is not to run in the opposite direction. A short tap is enough when timed correctly; holding the opposite key too long makes you accelerate away from the stop and begin moving the other way.
Counter-strafing is a ground shooting skill. Do not use the same idea blindly during a [[long-jump|long jump]], where reversing your input can change the flight path you are trying to preserve.

items: Moving right: tap A to brake.
Moving left: tap D to brake.
Watch for the moment your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] reaches zero before firing.
If you move the other way, shorten the tap rather than pressing harder.

sections.title: Crouch and duck input
sections.summary: Crouch changes player posture and can affect jump clearance and timing.

body.text: Crouching changes the player’s collision posture and the position of the model. A [[crouch-jump|crouch jump]] is useful for clearing geometry that a normal jump cannot reach, but the order and timing of jump and crouch inputs matter.

For ordinary ledge clearance, start with a straightforward jump followed by crouch while airborne. Then test release timing separately. Avoid mixing crouch-jump experiments with [[bhop|bhop]] or [[jumpbug|jumpbug]] drills until you can identify each input’s effect.

items: Test a normal jump and a [[crouch-jump|crouch jump]] on the same ledge.
Change only the crouch timing between attempts.
Keep duck-tap and double-duck results in the experimental category until reproduced on your target server.

sections.title: Approach setup and takeoff line
sections.summary: Prepare a route with a repeatable run-up, direction and takeoff point.

body.text: Pick a visible floor seam or map mark. Start from the same spot, move toward the edge and avoid last-second steering unless the route specifically needs it. Make the takeoff direction match the target rather than simply facing it with the camera.
Use [[velocity-momentum|[[velocity-momentum|velocity]]]] to compare attempts. If two jumps have different pre-speeds or different approach angles, they are not controlled comparisons.

items: Choose a fixed starting marker and a fixed target.
Keep the same movement keys during the run-up.
Record the takeoff position and horizontal speed.
Change only the run-up length or steering angle when testing.

keyCue.hint: Hold forward, then add a side key only when the route needs a curve.

sections.title: Diagonal ground movement
sections.summary: Combine forward and side inputs to move diagonally across the ground.

body.text: W, A, S and D are relative to your view. Pressing W+A creates a diagonal movement request; rotating the camera changes what those same keys mean in world space.

Diagonal input is useful for shaping a run-up and lining up with narrow platforms. It does not mean that holding more keys always gives more speed. Opposing keys can cancel or alter the desired movement direction.
Keep the view and route fixed while you test. Make one short diagonal movement, then compare it with a straight run and with an opposite-direction correction.

items: W+A moves forward-left relative to the view.
W+D moves forward-right.
S+A and S+D create backward diagonals.

categories.title: Vanilla air control
categories.intro: Steering and gaining speed once you are in the air.

sections.title: Air strafing
sections.summary: Steer and accelerate while airborne with a side key and matching mouse movement.

body.text: Air strafing lets you steer and build horizontal speed while airborne. The standard learning drill is: jump, release W, hold A while moving the mouse left, then release A and hold D while moving the mouse right. Keep the key and mouse direction matched during each phase.

The key controls the desired side acceleration; mouse movement changes the view-relative direction used by the air-movement calculation. Turning the mouse without the matching side key is not the same strafe. Holding A while turning right usually produces a poor or opposing input for the intended left strafe.

Start with broad, smooth arcs. A flick can turn your view faster than your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] can respond and may throw the landing line away. As you improve, shorten the arcs and change direction earlier. A successful strafe adds useful velocity while preserving the line toward the target.

items: Jump with W, then release W for the standard A/D drill.
Hold A and turn left together; release A before holding D and turning right.
Use a smooth mouse arc and watch both speed and landing line.
Avoid holding A and D together or adding S before the basic pattern is consistent.
Count useful strafes, not just the number of key presses.

sections.title: Strafe sync and mouse control
sections.summary: A good strafe keeps the directional input and mouse turn working together.

body.text: Sync is a movement-HUD or [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] measurement of how often the mouse turn and the selected A/D input line up with a useful acceleration direction. Different plugins can calculate or display it differently, so compare scores from the same tool and mode.

A high sync value is useful, but it is not a complete jump score. Takeoff speed, first-strafe timing, path curvature, strafe width, dead air, landing offset and the number of reversals all matter. A high-sync jump can still miss if the whole arc points away from the target.

Use the sync readout to identify a specific phase. If the first strafe scores well and the second does not, check the transition: release the first side key, reverse the mouse smoothly and press the other side key. Do not hold both keys while you are trying to reverse.

items: Compare attempts using the same [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] tool and server mode.
Review sync together with Pre, Max, distance and landing position.
Use the trace to identify which strafe loses speed.
Do not chase a high percentage at the expense of the landing line.

categories.intro: Jumps you can do on any official map.

sections.title: Normal jump and takeoff
sections.summary: A clean jump starts with predictable ground movement and a clear takeoff point.

body.text: A normal jump is the baseline for every other jump technique. Start with a controlled run, press jump once, and watch how the player rises, reaches the apex and falls back to the ground.

Your takeoff position, horizontal [[velocity-momentum|velocity]], surface and landing height all affect the result. For a fair comparison, practise from a flat surface to a target at the same elevation before adding gaps or sloped ground.
Once the normal jump is repeatable, add one variable: a side strafe, a crouch input, a different takeoff point or a different landing height. This makes it clear what the new input changed.

items: Mark a takeoff point and a landing target.
Practise without crouching first.
Keep the approach speed the same between attempts.

sections.title: Edge jump (EJ): takeoff at the ledge
sections.summary: A jump timed at the final usable ground contact on an edge.

body.text: An edge jump is a takeoff timed close to the end of a platform. The useful skill is controlling the final grounded moment and the direction of the takeoff. It is a route-timing technique, not the same thing as an [[edgebug|[[edgebug|edgebug]]]], which concerns a landing collision.

Approach the edge at a steady speed, keep the intended travel direction, and use a visual marker to repeat the takeoff point. A jump pressed too early wastes part of the platform; a jump pressed after ground contact has ended may become a fall instead.
The exact result depends on the platform collision and the movement state. Do not copy a fixed distance or tick count from a clip recorded on another map or build.

items: Use a visible edge marker and the same run-up.
Keep the camera and movement direction aligned with the target.
Compare early, clean-edge and late attempts.

sections.title: Bunny hop (bhop)
sections.summary: Chain jumps through consecutive landings using controlled air movement and correctly timed jump input.

body.text: A bunny hop chains a jump into the next landing. The basic loop is: jump, control the air path, prepare the next input, then jump again as the player lands. A scroll-wheel bind produces repeated jump presses, which gives you several input opportunities instead of one spacebar tap.

CS2 bhopping is not simply the old CS:GO “first grounded tick” rule. Valve’s 21 January 2026 update says landing time is calculated with subtick precision and that a jump press inside `sv_bhop_time_window`, centred on landing time, can count as a successful bhop if the jump-spam penalty has not rejected it. Valve also made legacy behaviour available for private servers through `sv_legacy_jump`. On 22 January, Valve clarified that landing vertical [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] affects landing speed penalties.

Community reverse-engineering by zer0k-z reports that jump presses that are too close together can be rejected by the jump-spam penalty. Its automated tests suggest a scroll interval around 16 ms performed well in its tested setup. Treat that as a measured starting point, not a Valve recommendation or a guaranteed setting for every server, input device and future build.

items: Start with one jump and one landing; do not begin by trying to chain ten hops.
Keep your A/D transition smooth and avoid changing several keys at touchdown.
Compare the result on the same server and map. Server settings can change the bhop rules, so record them with the attempt.
Do not use multi-action movement macros on official servers; Valve has restricted certain automated multi-input binds.

sections.title: Crouch jump and jump crouch
sections.summary: Two ways to combine crouch and jump, and why they differ.

body.text: A **crouch jump** means pressing crouch just before you jump. It gives you the most height and reaches boxes a normal jump cannot, such as the firebox on Mirage.
A **jump crouch** means jumping first, then crouching in the air. It tucks your legs up so your feet clear an edge, but it reaches less high than a crouch jump.
The firebox on Mirage needs both: crouch, jump, then crouch again in the air.
Valve servers ignore binds that do more than one action, so press crouch and jump yourself, crouch first and jump straight after.

sections.title: Air crouch
sections.summary: Crouching in the air to fit under things or land sooner.

body.text: An air crouch means crouching while you are in the air. It lets you duck under something you would otherwise hit, such as a doorframe. Crouching near the end of a jump also helps you land on far or tall spots more reliably, and makes some hard jumps easier and more consistent. The jump from mid to Ancient is possible without it, but harder.
Crouching late in a drop can shorten your fall, which players use for quiet drops and for landing on boxes faster.

keyCue.title: Air crouch

sections.title: Landing control and jump recovery
sections.summary: Land on the usable part of a surface and prepare the next movement without wasting the line.

body.text: A jump is not finished at the highest point. The landing surface, impact direction and room for the next movement decide whether the route continues. A landing near the centre of a platform is easier to recover from than a landing on a thin edge.
When chaining a route, know whether the next action is a new jump, a direction change, a crouch or a ladder contact. Avoid pressing several keys at the final moment without knowing which one matters.

For bhops, refer to the current CS2 landing/input timing described in [[bhop|the [[bhop|bhop]] section]]. Third-party movement overlays may report landing offsets differently, so check their own definitions before comparing results.

items: Aim for a repeatable landing zone.
Avoid turning sharply during the final part of the jump unless needed.
Use a full clip to review touchdown and the next input.

sections.title: Surf fundamentals
sections.summary: Ride angled surfaces by maintaining contact and shaping your exit velocity.

body.text: Surfing uses sloped collision surfaces to redirect movement while the player remains in contact with a ramp. The main task is to control the side of the player touching the ramp, maintain a stable line and leave the surface with a useful exit [[velocity-momentum|velocity]].

On a left or right ramp, use the side key that keeps the player pressed towards the ramp face while moving the mouse to shape the travel direction. The correct key depends on which side is in contact and the direction of travel. There is no safe “always hold A” or “always hold D” rule.

Start on a wide, shallow ramp. Learn to maintain contact without trying to chain ramps. Then practise the exit: aim for the next surface and use air control only after leaving the current ramp. Too much forward input can fight the sideways contact line; a hard mouse flick can throw you off the ramp.

Valve fixed incorrect surf air-acceleration clamping and a ramp-apex detection issue in November 2025. That is why old Source/CS:GO clips may differ from the current CS2 result. KZ slide ramps and resurfs are related route elements but belong in the dedicated KZ chapter, where server mode and course rules are specified.

items: Identify the side of the player touching the ramp.
Use a smooth contact line and small mouse corrections.
Learn the exit as a separate phase.
Avoid holding W through every ramp without checking the route.
Keep KZ slide-ramp and [[kz-resurf|resurf]] scoring separate from Vanilla surf practice.

keyCue.title: Surf
keyCue.hint: Press into the ramp with the corresponding side key.

sections.title: Surf exits and ramp-to-ramp transfers
sections.summary: Leave a ramp with a planned line and use air control to reach the next surface.

body.text: A [[surf-basics|surf]] transfer begins when you leave one ramp and travel through the air toward the next. Your exit speed and direction determine the available line. A large mouse turn at the last moment can send you past the target or make the next contact too shallow.

Look ahead to the next ramp and choose an exit path that gives you room to correct. Use [[air-strafing|air strafing]] between ramps, but do not make unnecessary direction changes when the target is already aligned.

sections.title: CS2KZ Vanilla and Classic modes
sections.summary: Understand the two CS2KZ modes before comparing movement or jumpstats.

body.text: CS2KZ documentation describes two movement modes. Vanilla (VNL) aims to preserve standard CS2 movement and applies quality-of-life features without changing movement-related settings. A VNL course is the closest KZ environment to practising matchmaking movement.

Classic (CKZ) is a separate movement ruleset intended to make KZ bhopping more consistent and less dependent on random landing outcomes. CS2KZ describes a logarithmic bhop speed formula: speed gains are larger at lower initial speeds and diminish as speed increases. The mode supports techniques such as [[kz-prekeep|pre-keep]] and WAD / “our father” tech that do not apply in the same way to VNL.

A record, jumpstat or route is only comparable when the mode matches. A 240-unit [[long-jump|long jump]] in VNL is not directly comparable with the same number in CKZ or an older GOKZ/KZTimer plugin. Check the server’s mode display and the course filter before you compare times or jumpstats.

Classic documentation and naming can evolve. The current CS2KZ website is the reference for the server’s active mode definition; old GOKZ pages describe Source/CS:GO plugin environments and should be treated as historical context unless the server explicitly says it uses those rules.

items: Check VNL or CKZ before starting a course.
Use VNL for the closest comparison with standard CS2 movement.
Use CKZ only when you intend to practise its separate bhop and [[kz-prekeep|pre-keep]] rules.
Do not compare records across modes without labelling them.

A course tier describes the challenge of the whole route. Higher tiers can combine [[pre-strafe|prestrafe]], long jumps, multi-strafing, bhops, slide ramps, resurfs, ladder jumps, wallstrafing and route sequencing. It is not a standalone rating for one trick.

sections.title: Pre-strafing
sections.summary: Build and preserve controlled takeoff velocity before a KZ jump.

body.text: In KZ, prestrafe is the controlled acceleration phase before takeoff. The goal is to build a useful horizontal [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and enter the jump at a predictable angle. KZ [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] records the speed at takeoff as `Pre`.

Your first strafe begins the moment you are airborne. A late first input wastes useful airtime; an overly sharp first turn can send you away from the block. The objective is not simply to turn as much as possible, but to convert your available air control into a useful path.

A box-tech jump uses a map’s block geometry as part of a route. A [[kz-slide-ramps|slide ramp]] uses an angled surface to preserve or redirect movement; a ressurf is a route-specific return to a [[surf-basics|surf]] surface after leaving it. The exact line depends on the map’s collision layout.

sections.title: Reading KZ jumpstats
sections.summary: Understand the pre-speed, max speed, sync, offset and distance values in a KZ jumpstat.

body.text: Jumpstats turn a jump into a set of measurements. The exact fields depend on the plugin and server mode, so read the HUD legend before comparing attempts. GOKZ documentation gives a useful legacy vocabulary, but its values and jump classifications were designed for its own plugin environment.

`Pre` is the speed at takeoff or ladder exit; `Max` is the highest speed during the jump; `Distance` is the measured horizontal jump distance; `Block` describes the gap or block context; `Edge` and `Deviation` describe where the jump begins and how it crosses the blocks. These values help distinguish a weak approach from a poor air path.

`Strafes` counts the movement turns or mouse-derived phases the plugin detects. `Sync` measures useful alignment between the mouse turn and A/D input. `OL` can show overlap between opposing keys; `DA` can show time with neither side key. `Width` describes the turn amount; `W release` and `Crouch release` compare release timing with the plugin’s expected reference.

Use stats to diagnose one phase at a time. Low Pre points to the approach; a good Pre but low Max may point to air input; good speed but a miss points to path or landing. Compare repeated attempts from the same start in the same mode.

items: Read the plugin’s legend and record the server mode.
Use Pre and Max to diagnose the approach and acceleration.
Use Strafes, Sync, OL and DA to review air input.
Use Height, Airtime and Offset to understand the jump arc.
Do not compare legacy GOKZ values with a different CS2KZ plugin as if they share one formula.

sections.title: Diagnosing speed loss

body.text: Speed loss can happen for different reasons. A poor run-up can lower takeoff speed; an uncoordinated air strafe can fail to add useful acceleration; a collision can redirect your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]; and extra grounded time can apply [[ground-acceleration-friction|friction]] or interrupt a bhop chain.

Do not fix all of these at once. First compare takeoff speed. If takeoff is low, work on the run-up and [[pre-strafe|prestrafe]]. If speed falls during flight, inspect the mouse-key timing and path. If the drop happens at landing, focus on the landing input and ground contact.
Use the same route and server settings across attempts. A patch, map change or server plugin change can invalidate an older baseline.

items: Check pre-speed before changing your air-strafe technique.
Look for the exact moment the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] changes.
Change one input variable at a time.

sections.title: Strafe count, sync, width and dead air
sections.summary: Use jumpstats to identify whether each air-strafe phase is gaining speed.

body.text: A [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] display can report how many strafes it detected, how well those strafes synced and how much time was spent overlapping or not holding a side key. The calculation is plugin-specific. In older GOKZ documentation, the number of strafes is calculated from mouse movement rather than a raw count of key presses.

Sync should describe useful acceleration, not simply fast mouse movement. A large turn can produce a low-value phase if the matching side key is wrong or if the player is already travelling at an angle that makes the turn unhelpful.

Strafe width describes how far the player turns during a phase. Wider turns are not always better: at higher speed, an excessive arc can bend the route away from the target. Dead air and overlap can expose poor transitions, but a non-zero value is not automatically a failure on every plugin or route.
Use the measurements to fix one issue: reduce overlap, improve the transition, adjust strafe width, or align the landing. Do not chase 100% sync if that makes the jump shorter or less repeatable.

items: Compare stats from the same plugin and mode.
Review the mouse trace alongside the A/D input overlay.
Change strafe width only after the direction sequence is consistent.
Use distance and landing position as the final outcome.

sections.title: KZ difficulty tiers and map reading
sections.summary: Use the CS2KZ tier system to choose a course and understand the skills it expects.

body.text: CS2KZ documents ten tiers. Its map guide describes the lower tiers as introductory courses and progressively adds multi-strafing, precise long jumps, harder [[kz-jumpstat-bh|bhop]] sequences, slide ramps, resurfs, ladder jumps, [[kz-box-tech|box-tech]] and wallstrafing.

The published descriptions are best-effort rather than rigid thresholds. A tier 4 course might include long jumps around the 260-unit range, but that does not mean every tier 4 jump must have that distance or that the number transfers to another movement mode.

Choose a map based on the skill it teaches, not just the tier number. If you are learning ladder exits, pick a course with repeatable ladder sections. If you are learning air control, practise a route that gives you room to recover.

items: Start with tier 1 or 2 if new to KZ.
Read the map and course description.
Check if the filter is VNL or CKZ.
Treat tier as a broad course difficulty, not a physics constant.

sections.title: KZ route review and repeatability
sections.summary: Review a full KZ route to identify the first movement phase that causes a failure.

body.text: A KZ route can combine [[pre-strafe|prestrafe]], long jumps, bhops, slides, resurfs, ladder jumps and map-specific tech. A failure at the final block may begin several sections earlier if an earlier landing changes your speed or position.

Review the route in order. Check the starting line-up, approach, takeoff speed, air-strfe path, landing offset and next input. Avoid changing the whole route at once; repeat the earliest failed section until it is stable.

For leaderboard attempts, record the course filter, mode, teleports setting and map version. CS2KZ course filters distinguish mode, teleports, tier and ranked status, so a time is meaningful only with its filter.

items: Find the first failed stage, not only the final miss.
Compare pre-speed and landing offset.
Practise the failed jump in isolation.
Reconnect the route once the isolated jump is stable.

sections.title: A structured movement practice routine
sections.summary: Separate the skills so each practice session has one clear objective.

body.text: A good practice route starts with low-complexity actions and adds one new skill at a time. A common progression is ground movement, [[counter-strafing|counter-strafing]], a single air strafe, alternating strafes, a normal jump, [[long-jump|long jump]] and finally a bhop chain.

Repeat each drill until the result is reasonably consistent. Do not use a single lucky attempt as proof that a technique is learned. Measure a small set of attempts and compare the average result or the number of successful repetitions.

When you move to advanced tricks, use a dedicated movement map with clear feedback. Avoid practising a precision collision exploit on a competitive map where the geometry and landing state are difficult to inspect.

items: Practise one mechanic per short block.
Record several attempts rather than only the best one.
Finish with a clean repetition, not a rushed final attempt.

sections.title: Mini-jumps and short-hop movement

body.text: “Mini-jump” is a community description rather than a separate Valve movement mode. Players use it for a low or short jump that clears a small obstacle while keeping the route compact.

The useful part is the route: takeoff speed, available headroom, jump input and landing space. A short hop is not automatically faster or more efficient than running; the obstacle and landing determine whether it helps.

items: Start with a low obstacle and enough landing space.
Try a normal jump first, then compare a shorter approach.

sections.title: Pixel surf: overview
sections.summary: A precision surf/contact technique that depends on tiny collision surfaces.

body.text: Pixel surfing is a community route term for maintaining or redirecting movement along a very small, often sloped collision face. The useful surface may be only a few units wide in the visible map, but the exact collision mesh determines whether a player can ride it.

The setup is a controlled entry angle and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. Approach the face so the player contacts the intended side, then use the matching side movement and mouse arc to stay aligned. If you hit the surface head-on, clip the wrong face or arrive too low, you may stop or fall instead of sliding.
Use a current recording with the collision surface visible. If you are documenting a route, include the exact map version, start point, approach speed, contact face, exit and repeated success rate.

items: Locate the actual collision face before practising.
Start slowly and adjust only the entry angle.
Watch the player’s contact and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] at the surface.
Retest after map updates.

sections.title: Pixel walking and pixel ledges
sections.summary: Standing on tiny or unintended collision surfaces created by map geometry.

body.text: Pixel walking means moving along a very narrow or unintended collision strip where the player can stand or travel despite the visible surface appearing too small. It is a map-geometry interaction, not a general acceleration technique.

The route depends on the actual collision mesh, player origin and edge tolerance. Some pixel-walk positions are useful for a movement route; others create unintended competitive positions and may violate tournament or server rules.

Check the specific event rules before using a pixel walk in a match. A workshop map can use intentional collision geometry, while a tournament map can prohibit the same kind of unintended ledge or pixel position. Record the map version and the exact standing location.

items: Check whether the position is intended by the map author.
Test the player’s foot placement, not just the camera position.
Do not use unintended pixel-walk positions in competition without checking the rules.
Retest after map clipping changes.

sections.title: Wall strafing: overview
sections.summary: Wall contact can change a path, but edge cases are patch-sensitive.

body.text: Wall strafing uses movement input and view direction while the player is close to a wall. The wall changes the collision constraint, so the useful path may involve sliding along the face or leaving it at an angle rather than moving through open air.

Start by approaching the wall at a shallow angle and identify which side of the player touches it. Use a side input and controlled mouse movement to keep the contact line. If you press into the wall at a steep angle, you can lose forward progress or end up with a different collision response.
Keep wall strafing separate from a [[wallbug|wallbug]] or ceiling head-bump. A wall strafe steers along a contact surface; a wallbug or head-bump relies on a particular collision event.

items: Approach at a shallow, repeatable angle.
Identify the wall-contact side.
Keep the mouse arc small while maintaining the contact line.
Compare the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] before, during and after wall contact.
Do not copy a route to a wall with a different normal or mesh.

sections.title: Wallbugs and wall-contact stops
sections.summary: Legacy Source collision interactions where a player becomes caught against angled geometry.

body.text: A wallbug is a community term for an unusual fall or collision response caused by pressing against a specific wall shape while descending. Some routes use the collision to slow, redirect or otherwise change the expected fall.

The result depends on the wall angle, adjacent face, player position, [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and the server’s movement build. A visual corner is not necessarily a collision corner, and a wall that works in one map may not work on another.

items: Use a known test map and a fixed drop height.
Check which wall face the player contacts.
Record the fall speed and the landing result.

sections.title: 360 bhop: rotation and air-control overview
sections.summary: A bhop route with a full view rotation; the spin itself is not proof of extra speed.

body.text: A 360 bhop combines a jump with a full view rotation and a controlled landing. The spin is a visual description, not the source of a free speed bonus. The player still has to manage the actual [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] vector, side-key input, airtime and final landing direction.

To practise the rotation, start with a normal jump and a wide landing area. Make a smooth turn while using A/D only when the air path needs steering. Do not spin the mouse as fast as possible: a full view rotation can leave the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] pointing away from the target even when the crosshair returns to its starting direction.

Advanced versions combine a 360 turn with a [[bhop|bhop]], a narrow plant or flowerpot landing, or a map-specific route. The landing surface and current game geometry decide whether the route is possible. A famous CS:GO-era attempt on Inferno flowerpots is not evidence that the same trick is a repeatable current CS2 route.

items: Learn a controlled turn on a wide landing area first.
Keep track of travel direction while rotating the camera.
Use A/D to shape the path, not to create a fake rotation boost.
Add a narrow landing only after the wide version repeats.
Retest map-specific routes after geometry patches.

sections.summary: A historical CS:GO-era Inferno 360 attempt; not a verified current CS2 route.

body.text: The famous Inferno flowerpot 360 reference is a historical CS:GO movement experiment. The 2023 write-up described a difficult attempt from the pallet area opposite the A-site flowerpots, using a 360-degree air turn and a bhop-style landing. The attempt was presented as extremely difficult and not reliably repeatable.

It is not a confirmed current CS2 route, and it should not be copied as a guaranteed method. CS2’s jump timing, movement updates and Inferno geometry have changed since that clip. Valve also modified the A balcony and nearby clipping in March 2026.

Use this section as a route-research example. To turn it into a real CS2 tutorial, capture a current uncut attempt showing the starting point, intermediate surfaces, key overlay, mouse movement, landing and multiple successful repeats. Until then, do not publish a precise input sequence as fact.

items: Keep the 2023 reference labelled as CS:GO history.
Do not attribute a successful CS2 completion to the old clip.
Retest the route on the current Inferno map.
Require a full input overlay and repeatable landings before writing exact steps.

sections.title: CS2 bhopping and movement patch history
sections.summary: A dated record of Valve changes that affect movement, bhopping, surfing and collision.

body.text: CS2 bhopping has changed since launch. Old CS:GO tutorials often describe tick-perfect landing rules that no longer match the current default game. Use this timeline when reviewing older clips or config advice.

items: 30 July 2025: Valve fixed a case where movement-button changes could be ignored while turning the view at very high frame rates, and a case where [[air-strafing|air strafing]] produced higher-than-usual [[velocity-momentum|velocity]].
1 August 2025: Valve fixed a [[bhop|bhop]] penalty that could keep accumulating when jump was not pressed, and changed the jump-spam clock to begin when the input registers.
17 September 2025: Valve improved timestep-independence for subtick movement acceleration.
4 November 2025: Valve fixed incorrect air-acceleration clamping while surfing and a ramp-apex identification issue.
21 January 2026: Valve moved landing-time calculation to subtick precision and changed the [[bhop|bhop]] acceptance window. `sv_legacy_jump` can restore legacy behaviour on private servers.
22 January 2026: Valve adjusted landing penalties so landing vertical [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] also affects the result.
24 August 2026: Valve fixed a case where player speed became too high when moving against walls.

body.text: These notes describe fixes and rule changes, not a list of guaranteed movement exploits. For the latest practical explanation of jump timing, read [[bhop|the current bhop section]] and the linked community reverse-engineering study in Sources.

Map geometry changes also matter. For example, Valve extended Inferno A balcony on 4 March 2026 and adjusted nearby clipping. Old route clips may begin or end on geometry that no longer exists in the same position.

sections.title: Jumpbug history
sections.summary: How jumpbugs changed after CS2 launched.

body.text: Early CS2 jumpbugs relied on binds or aliases that combined jump and crouch on one key. On 19 August 2024 Valve [made binds with more than one movement or attack action stop working](https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/730/view/6500469346429600836). Valve also changed jump heights in 2024 ([September](https://dust2.us/news/52569/valve-claims-to-fix-jump-bug-in-most-recent-update), [October](https://www.hltv.org/news/40150/valve-tackles-jump-bug-in-latest-cs2-update)), and rewrote jumping and landing on [21 January 2026](https://store.steampowered.com/news/posts/?appids=730&enddate=1773269954&feed=steam_community_announcements). Only certain drop heights work now, and the setup is harder than it was.
